speakerBio: Runs the neuro-ICU and treats anticoagulant reversal as a stat, minutes-matter intervention.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 72-year-old on warfarin collapses with a dense hemiplegia and a crushing headache; the CT lights up white in the basal ganglia. This is not a clot to dissolve — it is a bleed to contain, and the first hour is about pressure and reversal. Intracerebral haemorrhage is the deadliest stroke, and its early management is a race against the expanding haematoma.

1 · The mirror-image rule

Ischaemic stroke: leave the blood pressure high. Haemorrhagic stroke: bring it down and reverse the anticoagulation now. Same white-coat emergency, opposite reflex — the CT decides.

2 · Causes by pattern

Location / patternLikely cause
Deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum)Hypertensive (Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysm rupture)
Lobar (cortical, elderly)Cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Any, on a blood thinnerAnticoagulant-related
Young, unusual siteAVM, aneurysm, tumour, venous sinus thrombosis, drugs (cocaine)

3 · The target: haematoma expansion

Up to a third of ICHs expand in the first hours, and expansion drives death and disability. The two levers that limit it:

  • Intensive BP lowering: aim systolic to ~140 mmHg promptly and smoothly (INTERACT2, ATACH-2 — benefit from control, but avoid overly aggressive dips and large variability).
  • Urgent reversal of anticoagulation (below) — the single most time-critical action in an anticoagulated bleed.

4 · Reversal — know these by drug

AgentReversal
Warfarin4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K (not FFP if PCC available)
DabigatranIdarucizumab
Apixaban / rivaroxabanAndexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC
HeparinProtamine
AntiplateletsDo not routinely transfuse platelets — PATCH showed harm

5 · The rest of the bundle

  • Neurosurgery: evacuation is not routinely beneficial for most supratentorial ICH (STICH/STICH II), but is life-saving for cerebellar haemorrhage with deterioration/brainstem compression/hydrocephalus, and considered for accessible lobar clots and select minimally-invasive approaches.
  • ICP/oedema care (head up, osmotherapy), seizure treatment (not prophylaxis), reverse coagulopathy, and manage the airway.
  • Prognosis: the ICH score stratifies mortality — but beware early self-fulfilling pessimism; avoid premature DNAR/withdrawal in the first 24–72 hours.
☠️ M&M — the warfarin bleed reversed too late

A patient on warfarin with an ICH waited hours for "FFP to run through" while the INR stayed high and the haematoma doubled. PCC would have corrected the coagulopathy in minutes. Lesson: in an anticoagulated intracerebral haemorrhage, reversal is a stat, minutes-matter intervention — PCC + vitamin K for warfarin, the specific agent for a DOAC — given in parallel with BP control, not after a slow product.

6 · Take-home

  • ICH = lower the BP (~140 systolic) and reverse anticoagulation immediately — the mirror image of ischaemic stroke.
  • Deep = hypertensive; lobar elderly = amyloid.
  • Reversal: PCC + vitamin K (warfarin), idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet/PCC (Xa); no routine platelets (PATCH).
  • Surgery mainly for the deteriorating cerebellar bleed; avoid premature prognostic pessimism.

moderatorQs.q: What are the first two actions in an anticoagulated intracerebral haemorrhage?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Lower the blood pressure and reverse the anticoagulation — immediately and in parallel. Aim systolic to about 140 mmHg smoothly (INTERACT2/ATACH-2), and reverse the agent without delay: 4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet or PCC for the Xa inhibitors. These limit haematoma expansion, which is the main driver of death and disability.

moderatorQs.q: How does ICH management mirror ischaemic stroke?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It is the exact opposite reflex. In ischaemic stroke we allow permissive hypertension to perfuse the penumbra; in haemorrhage we lower the pressure to limit bleeding. In ischaemia we thin the blood; in haemorrhage we reverse anticoagulation and avoid antithrombotics. The non-contrast CT is what tells you which rulebook applies — which is why it is the first thing you do.

moderatorQs.q: When does ICH need a surgeon?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Routine evacuation of most supratentorial haemorrhage does not improve outcome (STICH/STICH II), but surgery is life-saving for a cerebellar haemorrhage with deterioration, brainstem compression or hydrocephalus, and is considered for accessible lobar clots and selected minimally-invasive approaches. So the classic surgical ICH is the deteriorating posterior-fossa bleed — recognise it early.

audienceQs.q: Should I give platelets if the patient is on aspirin?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — not routinely. The PATCH trial found platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated ICH caused harm (more death/dependency). Focus instead on BP control, reversing any true anticoagulant, and neurosurgical review. Platelets are reserved for genuine thrombocytopenia or planned neurosurgery.

audienceQs.q: How soon can we talk about prognosis and ceilings of care?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Cautiously, and not in the first day or two. Early prognostic pessimism becomes self-fulfilling — a premature DNAR or withdrawal can cause the poor outcome it predicts. Give aggressive early care, reassess over 24–72 hours, and use tools like the ICH score to inform rather than dictate conversations with family.
